title: Application of the Border Gateway Protocol in the Internet
summary: Describes how the Border Gateway Protocol is used in the Internet, as the companion to RFC 1771. It covers how BGP fits into inter-autonomous-system routing. It was a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains where and how the road-map swapping between big networks is used.

questions: how is bgp used in the internet
what does rfc 1772 say about route aggregation
subtitle: How BGP-4 is meant to be used between autonomous systems: topology, route aggregation, policy and path selection.

tldr.problem: The Internet was heading for scaling trouble: class-B address space running out and routing tables growing beyond what software and people could manage. BGP-4 needed a companion that says how to use it in that setting.
tldr.mechanism: The memo models the Internet as a graph of autonomous systems and describes BGP usage on it: neighbor relationships, mandatory route aggregation options, policy supplied as configuration, path selection criteria, interworking with EGP2 and BGP-3, and BGP and IGP consistency.
tldr.outcome: It is the usage guide that sits beside the BGP-4 specification (RFC 1771) and replaces RFC 1655. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes it.

today: RFC 1772 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1655, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the usage companion to RFC 1771, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: Why BGP-4 Needed a Usage Guide
sections.content:
This memo, together with its companion RFC 1771 (BGP-4), defines an inter-autonomous system routing protocol for the Internet. RFC 1771 is the protocol specification. This document describes how BGP is used in the Internet.

The text names three scaling problems: exhaustion of the class-B address space, routing tables growing beyond what software and people can manage, and eventual exhaustion of the 32-bit IP address space. It expects the first two to become critical within one to three years. Classless inter-domain routing (CIDR) is aimed at the first two. BGP-4 is an extension of BGP-3 that adds support for the route aggregation and reduction that CIDR relies on.

An autonomous system (AS) is treated as a set of routers under a single technical administration. It may use several interior gateway protocols and metrics inside, but to other AS's it must present one coherent routing plan and a consistent picture of which destinations are reachable through it.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was growing so fast that its address books and road maps were getting too big. BGP-4 helps keep them small, and this paper explains how to use it.

sections.title: The Topological Model and AS Types
sections.content:
A connection between two AS's means two things. There is a physical connection, a shared data link subnetwork on which each AS has at least one border gateway. And there is a BGP connection, a BGP session between BGP speakers in each AS. This memo adds a restriction: the BGP speakers must share the same data link subnetwork as the border gateways, so a session between adjacent AS's needs no support from inter-AS or intra-AS routing. Speakers do not have to be border gateways, and vice versa.

Traffic is either local traffic (the source or destination address belongs to a host inside the AS) or transit traffic (neither does). A major goal of BGP usage is to control the flow of transit traffic. That gives three kinds of AS: stub, multihomed and transit.

Because a full AS path suppresses routing loops and avoids the count-to-infinity problem of some distance vector algorithms, BGP imposes no topological restrictions on how AS's interconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: Some neighborhoods have one road out, some have several but will not let outsiders drive through, and some let through traffic pass. BGP helps each one decide which kind it wants to be.

sections.title: BGP in the Internet
sections.content:
Stub and multihomed AS's need not run BGP. They may use other protocols such as EGP to exchange reachability with transit AS's, and transit AS's using BGP tag that information as learned by some method other than BGP. The memo still recommends BGP for stub and multihomed AS's, because it gives better bandwidth and performance than protocols such as EGP, reduces the need for default routes, and gives multihomed AS's better inter-AS route choices.

Globally, BGP alone carries routing information between AS's, while both BGP and an IGP may carry information across an AS. Keeping the two consistent is called a significant issue and is covered in Appendix A.

Routers that talk BGP directly are BGP speakers. A peer in a different AS is an external peer, and a peer in the same AS is an internal peer. All speakers of one AS must give a consistent image of the AS to the outside, so they need consistent routing information and consistent policy constraints. External peers must be in different AS's but share a common data link subnetwork, and BGP across an intervening AS invalidates the AS path information.
sections.plainLanguage: Every big network picks some messengers to talk to the neighbors. All the messengers from one network must tell the same story, or the neighbors get confused.

sections.title: Route Aggregation Requirements
sections.content:
A conformant BGP-4 implementation is required to be able to specify when an aggregated route may be generated out of partial routing information. A speaker at an AS border must be able to generate an aggregate for a whole set of destination addresses (the NLRI, Network Layer Reachability Information) it controls, even if not all of them are reachable at once. An implementation is also required to be able to specify how NLRI may be de-aggregated.

When routes overlap, an implementation is required to support four options: install both the less and the more specific routes, install only the more specific, install only the less specific, or install neither.

Some policies depend on the NLRI, such as "research" versus "commercial", so a speaker that aggregates should be aware of what that does to routing policies where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of listing every house on a street, you can list just the street. The rules say a router must be able to do that, and must also be able to go back to listing houses when needed.

sections.title: Policy and Path Selection
sections.content:
Policies are not encoded in the protocol. They reach BGP as configuration information, and BGP enforces them by affecting path selection and by controlling redistribution of routing information. Examples: a multihomed AS can refuse to act as transit by advertising only routes to its own destinations, or can act as transit for a restricted set of neighbors. Fundamental to BGP is the rule that an AS advertises to neighbors only the routes that it uses, which reflects hop-by-hop routing.

Path selection is hard because there is no universally agreed metric among AS's, unlike a single hop count in RIP. A speaker keeps all feasible paths for a prefix but advertises only the primary one. Selection can be formalized as a function mapping each full AS path to a non-negative integer degree of preference, then choosing the highest. Possible criteria are AS count (smaller is generally better), policy compliance, presence or absence of certain AS's, path origin, AS path subsets and link dynamics. The text warns that criteria based on dynamic information can cause routing instability.

The memo does not standardize required policies, but strongly encourages implementors to support three: control announcements of BGP-learned routes to adjacent AS's, at least per address prefix and also per AS; let an AS prefer a path by assigning a degree of preference, at minimum based on the neighbor's IP address, in the range 0 to 2^31 - 1; and ignore routes with certain AS's in the AS_PATH attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network has its own rules for which roads it likes. It follows the best road it knows and only tells neighbors about roads it really uses itself.

sections.title: Interaction with EGP2 and BGP-3
sections.content:
An AS should advertise a minimal aggregate for its internal destinations relative to the address space it actually uses. A route carrying the ATOMIC_AGGREGATE attribute is not to be exported into BGP-3 or EGP2 unless that can be done without exploding the NLRI.

For graceful migration, a BGP-4 speaker may also take part in EGP2 or BGP-3. Information learned via EGP2 can be injected into BGP-4 with the ORIGIN attribute set to 1. When BGP-4 NLRI is injected into EGP2 or BGP-3, implementations are required to support three options: inject the default (0.0.0.0) only; allow controlled deaggregation of specific routes with export of non-aggregated NLRI; or export only non-aggregated NLRI.

Going into BGP-3, an AS_PATH containing AS_SET segments is rebuilt by treating them as AS_SEQUENCE segments. That loses set and sequence information but does not affect loop protection. Exchange with pure EGP2 or BGP-3 speakers may happen only at AS boundaries, and inside one AS all BGP conversations must be BGP-3 or BGP-4, not a mixture.
sections.plainLanguage: When a town switches to a new map format, some neighbors still use the old one. This part says how to translate between them without losing the way.

sections.title: Running BGP over Switched Virtual Circuits
sections.content:
On switched virtual circuit (SVC) subnetworks it can be useful to avoid keeping circuits permanently open and to eliminate periodic KEEPALIVE messages. The feature is selected by specifying a zero Hold Time in the OPEN message. It suits only BGP speakers directly connected over a common virtual circuit.

To compensate for the missing keepalives, the circuit manager must be able to detect link layer unreachability in a predictable finite period. On failure it should start a configurable dead timer and try to re-establish the link. If the timer expires it sends an internal DEAD indication to TCP, and if the link returns it cancels the timer and sends UP. TCP needs a small modification: DEAD flushes the transmit queue and aborts the connection, and UP transmits queued data or lets an outgoing call proceed.

If the BGP process and circuit manager can fail separately, a periodic two-way poll between them should be implemented, and each closes its related connections if it finds the other gone.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally two routers keep saying "still here?" to each other. On a phone-style link you can skip that if the phone line itself tells you when the call drops.

sections.title: Keeping BGP and the IGP Consistent
sections.content:
Appendix A is informational: the methods are not proposed as part of standard BGP usage. The problem is timing. A border gateway may learn a new BGP route before the IGP can carry transit traffic to the exit gateway, and during that window incorrect routing or black holes can occur. So a border gateway should not advertise a route via an exit gateway to external peers until interior routing has converged on that exit.

Techniques described are: carrying BGP information through the IGP, when the IGP floods completely and converges in one pass; a tagged IGP whose tags identify the exit border gateway, with two rules about when to propagate reachability and that unreachability must be propagated immediately; encapsulation of transit traffic in datagrams addressed to the exit gateway; and pervasive BGP, where every router speaks BGP and does a recursive lookup.

For IGPs such as RIP that can neither carry nor tag BGP information, the rules are weaker: unreachability goes out immediately, and reachability only after the IGP route exists and enough time has passed to converge. If IGP convergence is under some small value X, probably less than one second, the issue can be ignored at the cost of brief instability.
sections.plainLanguage: Before telling the neighbors to send you mail for a faraway street, make sure your own mail carriers already know the way there. Otherwise letters get lost.
